due.e: From Middle English dewe, dew, due, from Old French deü (“due”), past participle of devoir (“to owe”), from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”), from dē- (“from”) + habeō (“to have”).

dug.e: From earlier dugge ("pap, teat"; compare also English dialectal ducky, dukky (“the female breast”)), apparently connected to Danish dægge (“to suckle”), Swedish dägga (“to suck”), Old English dēon (“to suckle”).
dug.g: A mammary gland on a domestic mammal with more than two breasts, mostly used to refer to the nipples of non-ruminants and non-primates.

duke.e: From Old French duc, through Middle English duk, duke, from Latin dux, ducis. Was present as duc in late Old English, from the same Latin source. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-, which is also the source of the second component in German Herzog. The “fist” sense is thought to be Cockney rhyming slang where “Duke(s) of York” = fork.
duke.g: The male ruler of a duchy (female equivalent: duchess).

dulcimer.e: From Old French doulcemelle, probably from Latin dulce melos (“sweet song”), from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “melody, song”).
dulcimer.g: A stringed instrument, with strings stretched across a sounding board, usually trapezoidal, played by plucking on the strings (traditionally

dull.e: From Middle English dull, dul (also dyll, dill, dwal), from Old English dol (“dull, foolish, erring, heretical; foolish, silly; presumptuous”), from Proto-West Germanic *dol, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz, from earlier *dwulaz, a variant of *dwalaz (“stunned, mad, foolish, misled”).
dull.g: Lacking the ability to cut easily; not sharp.

dull.e: Probably from Irish dul, dol (“loop, noose, snare”).
dull.g: A noose of string, metal wire, or hair used to snare an animal, especially a fish.

dumb.e: From Middle English dumb (“silent, speechless, mute, ineffectual”), from Old English dumb (“silent, speechless, mute, unable to speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *dumb, from Proto-Germanic *dumbaz (“dull, dumb”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, smoke, darken, obscure”).
dumb.g: Unable to speak; lacking power of speech.

dumb.e: From Middle English dumben, from Old English *dumbian (found in the compound ādumbian (“to become mute or dumb; keep silence; hold one’s peace”)), from Proto-Germanic *dumbijaną, *dumbōną (“to be silent, become dumb”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, smoke, darken, obscure”).

dump.e: From Middle English dumpen, dompen, probably from Old Norse dumpa (“to thump”) (whence Danish dumpe (“to fall suddenly”)), of uncertain origin, possibly imitative of falling, similar to thump.
dump.g: A place where waste or garbage is left; a ground or place for dumping ashes, refuse, etc.; a disposal site.

dung.e: From Middle English dung, dunge, donge, from Old English dung (“dung; excrement; manure”), from Proto-West Germanic *dungu, from Proto-Germanic *dungō (“dung”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ- (“to cover”). Superseded non-native Middle English fen (“dung, excrement, filth”), from Old French fien, fiente (“dung, manure”).

dung.g: Alternative spelling of dong (“sound of a bell”).

dungeon.e: From Middle English dongeoun (“keep of a castle; dungeon; abyss, cave, den; whirlpool”), from Anglo-Norman donjun (“keep of a castle; keep used as a prison; dungeon”) and continental Old French donjon (“keep of a castle”).
dungeon.g: An underground prison or vault, typically built underneath a castle.

dunghill.e: From Middle English donghil. By surface analysis, dung + hill.
dunghill.g: A heap of dung, especially one for agricultural purposes.

duplicity.e: From Latin duplicare (double). Equivalent to duplex + -ity.

durable.e: From Middle English durable, from Old French durable, from Latin dūrābilis (“lasting, permanent”), from dūrō (“harden, make hard”).
durable.g: Able to resist wear or decay; lasting; enduring.

duration.e: From Middle English duracioun, from late Old French duracion, from Medieval Latin dūrātiō.
duration.g: An amount of time or a particular time interval.

dure.e: From Middle English duren (“to last”), from Old French durer, from Latin dūrō, dūrāre.

during.e: From Middle English during, durynge, durinde, durand, durende, present participle of duren (“to last”), equivalent to dure + -ing.
during.g: For all of a given time interval; throughout; in; pending.

dusk.e: From Middle English dosk, dusk(e) (“dusky”, adj.), from Old English dox (“dark, swarthy”), from Proto-Germanic *duskaz (“dark, smoky”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwes-, related to *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, mist, haze”).
dusk.g: Tending to darkness or blackness; moderately dark or black; dusky.

dusk.e: From Middle English dusken, from Old English doxian.
dusk.g: To begin to lose light or whiteness; to grow dusk.

dust.e: From Middle English dust, doust, from Old English dūst (“dust, dried earth reduced to powder; other dry material reduced to powder”), from the fusion of Proto-Germanic *dustą (“dust”) and *dunstą (“mist, dust, evaporation”), both from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, raise dust”).

duty.e: From Middle English duete, from Middle English dewe + Middle English -te. Equivalent to due + -ty.
duty.g: That which one is morally or legally obligated to do.

dare.e: From Middle English durren, from Old English durran, from Proto-West Germanic *durʀan, from Proto-Germanic *durzaną (“to dare”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰedʰórse (“to dare”), reduplicated stative of the root *dʰers- (“to be bold, to dare”), an *-s- extension of *dʰer- (“to hold, support”).
dare.g: To have enough courage (to do something).

dare.e: From Middle English daren, from Old English darian.
dare.g: To stare stupidly or vacantly; to gaze as though amazed or terrified.
